tier_reason: The lzbench 2.4 table does list lizard 2.1 -29 at 1470 MB/s decompress, 32.41% vs zlib 1.3.2 -9 at 318 MB/s, 31.92% (gcc 15.2.0, EPYC 9555P, single thread), but lzbench and Lizard share one maintainer (inikep), so this is not an independent third-party measurement; the Lizard README table (lzbench 2.0, gcc 14.2.0, EPYC 9554) is first-party too, and neither page states compile flags (only implicit in the public lzbench Makefile), so C rather than B or A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P, gcc 15.2.0): lizard 2.1 -29 decompress 1470 MB/s at ratio 32.41% (compress 2.08 MB/s) vs zlib 1.3.2 -9 318 MB/s at 31.92% (4.6x, derived from page data); vs zstd 1.5.7 -1 1351 MB/s at 34.53% (1.09x, derived from page data). Lizard README (lzbench 2.0, EPYC 9554, GCC 14.2.0, Ubuntu 24.04.1): lizard 2.1 -10 2161 MB/s at 48.79% vs zstd 1.5.6 -1 1342 MB/s at 34.64%.
corrections.caveats: README admits LZ4 and zstd have advanced so much that Lizard is outdated and effectively obsolete; lz4 1.10.0 decompresses faster (3832 MB/s in lzbench 2.4) than every Lizard level. The margin over zstd -1 is small and the high-ratio levels compress at about 2 MB/s; the real win is decompression vs zlib. The benchmark suite is maintained by Lizard's own author.

notes: Last commit 2025-10-09 (fix for Lizard_writeBlock with a one-byte input), within 12 months of today, so maintenance_status corrected from stale to active despite the author calling the codec obsolete. License BSD-2-Clause and 711 stars confirmed.

tier_reason: The independent, well-known lzbench suite (public code, gcc 15.2.0 release binary, single thread of an EPYC 9555P) lists lzsse8 2019-04-18 -6 at 5007 MB/s decompress, 35.61% and lzsse4 -6 at 4714 MB/s, 35.91% vs lz4hc 1.10.0 -12 at 3813 MB/s, 36.45%; compile flags are not stated on the page (only implicit in the Makefile), so B, not A, consistent with other lzbench-based entries.

corrections.claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P): lzsse8 -6 decompress 5007 MB/s at ratio 35.61% vs lz4hc 1.10.0 -12 3813 MB/s at 36.45% (1.31x, derived from page data); lzsse4 -6 4714 MB/s at 35.91%. Compression is slow (about 9 MB/s at -6). The repo README itself gives no current numbers.
corrections.caveats: Repo says its blog-post figures are out of date; numbers here come from lzbench. Decompress-only win (compression about 9 MB/s at the optimal-parse levels), 64-bit x86 with SSE4.1 only; lzbench notes lzsse8fast has a bug (ConorStokes/LZSSE issue #14). Plain lz4 1.10.0 decodes at 3832 MB/s, close to lzsse2.

notes: License BSD-2-Clause, 151 stars, last commit 2019-04-18 (1847c3e, the version lzbench integrates); abandoned status correct. The blog posts on conorstokes.github.io are on a blocked host and were not opened.

tier_reason: The independent lzbench 2.4 table (public code, gcc 15.2.0, single thread of an EPYC 9555P) lists misa77 0.6.0 -1 at 73.8 MB/s compress, 7813 MB/s decompress, 42.65% vs lz4 1.10.0 at 550 / 3832 MB/s, 47.60%; flags are not stated on the page, so B. The README's own lzbench runs (i7-14650HX turbo off, Apple M3) name no compiler or flags, so they alone would be C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (Intel i7-14650HX, turbo off): level 1 decompress 5376 MB/s at 42.64% vs LZ4 1.10.0 2514 MB/s at 47.59% (2.1x, derived from page data); vs zstd 1.5.7 -1 903 MB/s at 34.54%. lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P): misa77 0.6.0 -1 decompress 7813 MB/s at 42.65% vs lz4 1.10.0 3832 MB/s at 47.60% (2.0x, derived from page data); compress 73.8 MB/s vs lz4 550 MB/s.

notes: README numbers and lzbench rows match the record; MIT license, 172 stars, last commit 2026-08-10 confirmed. misa77 was merged into lzbench recently (0.6.0 dated 2026-07-30), so the lzbench run is by the suite maintainer, not the misa77 author.
